back: The potential difference across the membrane of a neurone not transmitting an impulse: about −70 mV, inside negative.
A rapid, temporary reversal of membrane potential (about −70 mV to about +30 to +40 mV and back) caused by voltage-gated ion channels.

front: What does the sodium-potassium pump move per ATP?
Why is the resting membrane more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺?
back: Some K⁺ channels are open at rest while voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are closed; K⁺ diffuses out, leaving the inside negative.

front: Ion movements in depolarisation and repolarisation
back: Depolarisation: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ in. Repolarisation: Na⁺ channels close, voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, K⁺ out.
Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are slow to close, so too much K⁺ leaves; potential overshoots to about −80 mV.
If threshold is reached a full-sized action potential always occurs; below threshold none occurs.
The time after an action potential when another cannot be produced (absolute) or needs a stronger stimulus (relative).

front: Why is a receptor called a **transducer**?
back: It converts the energy of a stimulus into an electrical change (receptor potential).
